title: Ba bạn bàn về bức tranh tường cũ của trường
transcript:
A: So the council has offered some money to repaint the mural on the gym wall, and honestly, I can't decide how I feel about it.
B: What is there to decide? It's peeling off in sheets, Maya. Half the fish have lost their tails, and the sun, well, the sun is just a pale smudge now.
A: I know, I know. But my grandfather helped paint that wall thirty years ago, or maybe it was thirty-five. Either way, painting over it feels like erasing him.
C: Can I say something slightly uncomfortable? I think what you're protecting is the memory, not the mural. Those aren't the same thing.
A: That's easy for you to say, Tessa. You've only been at this school since September.
C: Fair enough. But newcomers sometimes see a wall more clearly. And what I see is a picture that's quietly teaching everyone that nobody here cares about maintenance.
B: Ha! That's rather harsh, but it does make me wonder. What if we photograph every inch of it first, so the original is properly preserved, and then repaint it from the photographs?
C: A copy, though. Faithful, perhaps, but still a copy. I'd rather the students designed something new, using the old fish as a starting point.
B: Of course you would. Last year you also wanted to replace the school crest with a more inclusive symbol, and look how well that went.
C: I was outvoted by a landslide, yes. I remember it vividly, thank you.
A: Okay, so what if there's a compromise? We keep one corner untouched, as a sort of window into the past, and the rest becomes new work.
B: A corner of peeling paint next to a fresh mural. That sounds either very brave or very ugly.
A: Possibly both. But I could live with brave and ugly more easily than with a spotless wall that's forgotten who made the first one.
C: Then put your grandfather's name in that corner. A small plaque. I'll even write to the council about the funding, if you like.
B: Fine, fine. But when that corner starts flaking again, I'm going to say I told you so, loudly, in assembly.

questions.prompt: True, False, or Not given? Maya's grandfather painted the whole mural on his own.
choices: True
False
Not given
questions.explanation: Maya nói ông chỉ 'helped paint that wall', tức là góp tay chứ không vẽ một mình.
choiceExplanations: Sai — 'True': Maya không nói ông vẽ một mình.
Đúng — Maya nói 'my grandfather helped paint that wall', nghĩa là ông chỉ là một trong số những người cùng vẽ.
Sai — 'Not given': Bài có nói rõ vai trò của ông nên không phải 'Not given'.

questions.prompt: What is Tessa's main point in her first long comment?
choices: The mural should never have been painted on a school wall.
Maya's strong feelings are really about a memory rather than the painting itself.
Maya is too young to have a say in the decision.
The council has not offered enough money for the repairs.
questions.explanation: Tessa phân biệt giữa ký ức và bức tranh: 'I think what you're protecting is the memory, not the mural.'
choiceExplanations: Sai — 'The mural should never have been painted on a school wall.': Tessa không phản đối việc có bức tranh; bạn ấy chỉ nói rằng điều Maya đang bảo vệ là ký ức.
Đúng — Tessa nói 'what you're protecting is the memory, not the mural'.
Sai — 'Maya is too young to have a say in the decision.': Không ai nói Maya quá nhỏ để quyết định; chính Maya mới là người nhắc rằng Tessa chỉ ở trường từ tháng Chín.
Sai — 'The council has not offered enough money for the repairs.': Không ai bàn xem số tiền của hội đồng có đủ hay không; Tessa chỉ nhắc tiền khi hứa viết thư xin kinh phí cho tấm bảng.

questions.prompt: What does Speaker B's remark about the school crest suggest?
choices: Speaker B admires Tessa for her bold and inclusive ideas.
Speaker B wants to replace the crest with a new symbol as well.
The crest is more important to the school than the mural.
Tessa's proposals for change have a history of being unpopular.
questions.explanation: Câu 'look how well that went' mang giọng mỉa mai, ngụ ý đề xuất trước đây của Tessa thất bại.
choiceExplanations: Sai — 'Speaker B admires Tessa for her bold and inclusive ideas.': Giọng của B là mỉa mai ('and look how well that went'), không phải ngưỡng mộ.
Sai — 'Speaker B wants to replace the crest with a new symbol as well.': Chính Tessa là người từng muốn đổi huy hiệu; B chỉ nhắc chuyện đó để trêu.
Sai — 'The crest is more important to the school than the mural.': Không ai so sánh tầm quan trọng của huy hiệu và bức tranh.
Đúng — B nhắc chuyện huy hiệu để trêu: Tessa đáp 'I was outvoted by a landslide', ngụ ý những đề xuất thay đổi của bạn ấy thường không được ủng hộ.

questions.prompt: How does Speaker B feel about the final compromise?
choices: He accepts it but expects it to cause problems later.
He is delighted and offers to pay for the plaque.
He still refuses to agree to any plan at all.
He thinks the plan is brave and wants a bigger old corner.
questions.explanation: 'Fine, fine. But ... I'm going to say I told you so' cho thấy B miễn cưỡng đồng ý và đoán trước rắc rối.
choiceExplanations: Đúng — B nói sẽ 'say I told you so, loudly, in assembly' khi góc tranh cũ bong tróc, tức là chấp nhận nhưng không tin tưởng.
Sai — 'He is delighted and offers to pay for the plaque.': B không nhắc việc trả tiền cho bảng tưởng niệm; Tessa mới là người hứa viết thư xin kinh phí.
Sai — 'He still refuses to agree to any plan at all.': B nói 'Fine, fine', tức là đã đồng ý.
Sai — 'He thinks the plan is brave and wants a bigger old corner.': B chỉ gọi nó là 'brave or ugly' và không đòi mở rộng góc tranh cũ.

title: Phỏng vấn nhà sinh thái học về cái ao của trường
transcript:
A: Welcome back to Science Corner. Today we're talking about the school pond, which, I'm told, has become the scene of a minor ecological crime. Dr. Reyes, what happened?
B: Well, crime is a little dramatic, though I do appreciate the drama. Someone, and we may never know who, emptied a home aquarium into the pond about two summers ago. A few small turtles went in, along with some very fast-growing water plants. Within a season, the plants had covered most of the surface.
A: And that's bad because?
B: Because underneath that green carpet there's no light. The native plants die, the insects that depend on them disappear, and then the frogs have nothing left to eat. It's a chain, and the plants are the first link.
A: So the turtles are the villains?
B: Not at all, and this is what students often get wrong. The turtles are mostly innocent bystanders. They eat a little, but the plants are the real problem. Though, to be honest, I assumed the opposite when I first arrived. I had to be corrected by a ten-year-old with a notebook.
A: Wonderful. So what's the plan?
B: We have two options. We can pull the plants out by hand, which is slow but cheap and gentle, or we can use a chemical treatment, which is quick but might harm the very frogs we're trying to protect. I've recommended the first.
A: And how long will that take?
B: With thirty volunteers working every Saturday, I'd say until the end of spring. Ask me again in March and I'll probably say April.
A: Ha! And the turtles?
B: They'll be moved to a rescue center. Which, incidentally, has asked us not to publish its location, so please don't ask me.
A: Wouldn't dream of it. Any message for our listeners before we go?
B: Just one. If you can't keep a pet any more, call an animal shelter. A pond is not a retirement home, however peaceful it looks.
A: On that note, thank you, Dr. Reyes.
B: My pleasure. And thank you for not calling it a crime scene on air. Twice.

questions.prompt: How does Dr. Reyes react to the host's word 'crime'?
choices: He is offended and demands an apology.
He agrees that someone should be punished.
He is amused but thinks it exaggerates the situation.
He thinks the problem is too minor to discuss.
questions.explanation: Ông chỉnh nhẹ cách nói của người dẫn nhưng vẫn vui vẻ.
choiceExplanations: Sai — 'He is offended and demands an apology.': Ông vẫn đùa ở cuối bài; không có dấu hiệu bị xúc phạm.
Sai — 'He agrees that someone should be punished.': Ông nói 'we may never know who' và không đề cập đến việc trừng phạt.
Đúng — Ông nói 'crime is a little dramatic, though I do appreciate the drama', vừa thấy buồn cười vừa cho là hơi quá.
Sai — 'He thinks the problem is too minor to discuss.': Ông gọi đó là vấn đề thật và đang dẫn đầu kế hoạch xử lý.

questions.prompt: How did Dr. Reyes's opinion of the turtles change?
choices: He first liked them, then found they ate all the frogs.
He always believed they were harmless to the pond.
He first blamed them, then learned the plants did more damage.
He never had an opinion until the interview.
questions.explanation: Ông từng cho rùa là thủ phạm, sau đó được 'a ten-year-old with a notebook' sửa lại.
choiceExplanations: Sai — 'He first liked them, then found they ate all the frogs.': Bài nói rùa 'eat a little' và không ăn hết ếch.
Sai — 'He always believed they were harmless to the pond.': Ông thừa nhận mình từng nghĩ ngược lại.
Đúng — Ông nói 'I assumed the opposite when I first arrived' rồi được một em nhỏ chỉnh lại.
Sai — 'He never had an opinion until the interview.': Ông kể mình đã có suy nghĩ ban đầu khi mới đến.

questions.prompt: True, False, or Not given? The rescue center is close to the school.
choices: True
False
Not given
questions.explanation: Ông chỉ nói trung tâm cứu hộ yêu cầu không công bố vị trí; không có thông tin về khoảng cách.
choiceExplanations: Sai — 'True': Bài không cho biết trung tâm ở gần.
Sai — 'False': Bài cũng không cho biết trung tâm ở xa.
Đúng — Vị trí trung tâm cứu hộ được giữ kín nên không có thông tin về khoảng cách.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of Dr. Reyes's final message?
choices: To discourage people from putting unwanted pets in ponds
To ask listeners to buy chemical treatments for ponds
To advertise the volunteer days on Saturdays
To praise people who keep turtles at home
questions.explanation: Lời nhắn cuối cảnh báo không thả thú nuôi xuống ao.
choiceExplanations: Đúng — Ông nói nếu không nuôi nổi thú cưng thì hãy gọi nơi cứu hộ, vì ao 'is not a retirement home'.
Sai — 'To ask listeners to buy chemical treatments for ponds': Ông chỉ nhắc hóa chất như một phương án nhanh nhưng có thể hại ếch, và đã đề xuất nhổ cây bằng tay.
Sai — 'To advertise the volunteer days on Saturdays': Ông chỉ nhắc tình nguyện viên khi kể kế hoạch, không phải lời nhắn cuối.
Sai — 'To praise people who keep turtles at home': Ông không khen việc nuôi rùa; ông khuyên không thả chúng đi.

title: Bài giảng về cách thành phố giảm tiếng ồn
transcript:
A: Right, let's pick up where we left off. Last week I argued that noise isn't merely annoying, it's a form of pollution, and today I want to look at what cities have actually tried. I'll go through three approaches, and I'd like you to decide which one you'd defend in an exam.
A: First, the obvious one: make things quieter at the source. Quieter road surfaces, electric buses, rules about when building work can start. It sounds sensible, and it usually is, but it's expensive, and the results arrive slowly. A new road surface wears out, and then you're back where you started.
A: Second, put something in the way. Walls beside motorways, thick hedges, double-glazed windows. Now, this is where people get a little carried away. A wall does reduce sound, certainly, but it also just pushes the problem sideways. The residents behind the wall are happy, and the ones across the valley, who now hear the echo, are not. Nobody puts that on the brochure.
A: Third, and this is my personal favorite, change what people expect to hear. Some cities have added fountains and planted trees in squares, not because trees block much sound, they don't, but because people judge a place by how it feels, and a pleasant sound can make a loud one seem less irritating. I wouldn't call that a solution, exactly. It's more of a clever distraction. But it's cheap, and apparently it works.
A: Now, you might be thinking, why not simply ban the noisy things? Well, a city without any noise is a city with no traffic, no markets and no children, and I doubt any of us would enjoy living there. The question isn't whether to have noise, but whose noise, and when.
A: For next time, I'd like you to measure the sound level outside your own building at three different hours. Don't worry about being scientific. A phone application is fine. Just write down what surprised you, and I mean genuinely surprised, not what you think I'd like to hear.

questions.prompt: What does the lecturer say about walls beside motorways?
choices: They are the cheapest and most reliable solution of all.
They completely remove noise for everyone nearby.
They are mainly built to improve the view.
They help some residents but can create new problems for others.
questions.explanation: Tường chặn âm chỉ chuyển vấn đề sang chỗ khác.
choiceExplanations: Sai — 'They are the cheapest and most reliable solution of all.': Bài giảng không gọi tường là giải pháp rẻ hay đáng tin nhất.
Sai — 'They completely remove noise for everyone nearby.': Người bên kia thung lũng vẫn nghe tiếng vọng.
Sai — 'They are mainly built to improve the view.': Bài không nhắc đến cảnh quan.
Đúng — Giảng viên nói người sau tường hài lòng còn người bên kia thung lũng nghe tiếng vọng: 'pushes the problem sideways'.

questions.prompt: What is the lecturer's attitude to the third approach, using fountains and trees?
choices: Enthusiastic, because trees block most of the sound.
Mildly skeptical, but she admits it is cheap and seems effective.
Scornful, because it has never worked anywhere.
Indifferent, since she has not read about it.
questions.explanation: Cô vừa nghi ngờ (không phải 'solution') vừa thừa nhận hiệu quả và chi phí thấp.
choiceExplanations: Sai — 'Enthusiastic, because trees block most of the sound.': Cô nói rõ cây 'don't' chặn được nhiều âm thanh.
Đúng — Cô gọi nó là 'more of a clever distraction' nhưng 'it's cheap, and apparently it works'.
Sai — 'Scornful, because it has never worked anywhere.': Cô nói 'apparently it works'.
Sai — 'Indifferent, since she has not read about it.': Cô gọi đó là phương án yêu thích cá nhân và bàn khá chi tiết.

questions.prompt: True, False, or Not given? The lecturer has already measured the noise level outside her own building.
choices: True
False
Not given
questions.explanation: Bài giảng chỉ giao bài đo mức ồn cho sinh viên; không nói giảng viên đã tự đo ở tòa nhà của mình.
choiceExplanations: Sai — 'True': Bài không nói giảng viên đã tự đo.
Sai — 'False': Bài cũng không nói giảng viên chưa đo.
Đúng — Giảng viên chỉ yêu cầu sinh viên đo; không có thông tin về việc cô tự đo.

questions.prompt: What does the lecturer ask the students to do for next time?
choices: Write a scientific report using professional equipment.
Interview neighbors about how they feel about traffic.
Prepare to defend one approach in an exam next week.
Record honest observations of the sound outside their building at different times.
questions.explanation: Bài tập là đo ba lần và ghi lại điều thực sự bất ngờ.
choiceExplanations: Sai — 'Write a scientific report using professional equipment.': Cô nói 'Don't worry about being scientific' và dùng ứng dụng điện thoại là đủ.
Sai — 'Interview neighbors about how they feel about traffic.': Bài không yêu cầu phỏng vấn hàng xóm.
Sai — 'Prepare to defend one approach in an exam next week.': Cô nhắc chuyện bảo vệ phương án trong kỳ thi chỉ như gợi ý khi nghe giảng.
Đúng — Cô yêu cầu đo mức ồn ba lần khác nhau và ghi lại điều thực sự gây bất ngờ.

title: Điểm nhóm hay điểm cá nhân cho dự án
transcript:
A: Welcome to this week's debate, where two of our best speakers argue about group projects. The question: should every member of a team receive the same grade? Nathan, you're first.
B: Thank you. I'll be direct. A shared grade is the only fair system, because the whole point of a group project is that the team succeeds or fails together. In real jobs nobody gets a separate result for the part of the bridge they built.
C: I'm tempted to say that bridges are a poor example, but let me start more politely. Nathan, I admire the principle. In practice, though, a shared grade rewards the person who does nothing. We all know one, and he usually sits near the back and offers moral support.
B: Moral support is underrated.
C: Not by the person who stayed up until two in the morning finishing her slides. And I'm not exaggerating, that was actually me, and it was ten past two, not two.
B: Fine, but think about what individual grades do. Suddenly everyone is guarding their own territory. Nobody helps a struggling teammate, because helping doesn't earn them anything. You turn cooperation into bookkeeping.
C: That's a fair worry. So perhaps there's a hybrid. Perhaps most of the mark is shared, but a smaller part comes from a short form where team members honestly describe who did what.
B: And then every team in the school quietly agrees to rate each other highly so nobody gets into trouble. I've seen it. Honesty is wonderful, but it doesn't survive a deadline.
C: Which is why teachers would have to read the forms critically, not just add up the numbers.
B: In which case, they'd need more time than they have. I'd trust a teacher's overall impression long before I'd trust a form.
C: Interesting. So you're not quite defending equal grades anymore, you're defending the teacher's judgment.
B: Perhaps I am. I'd rather say I'm defending whichever method hurts the fewest people.
A: Well, on that note, I think we've arrived somewhere neither of you planned. Let's hear from the audience.

questions.prompt: What is Nathan's main argument at the start of the debate?
choices: Individual grades are impossible to calculate.
A team should share one grade because it succeeds or fails together.
Teachers should not give any marks for projects.
Students prefer working alone to working in a team.
questions.explanation: Luận điểm mở đầu của Nathan là điểm chung vì cả nhóm cùng thành bại.
choiceExplanations: Sai — 'Individual grades are impossible to calculate.': Nathan không nói việc tính điểm cá nhân là bất khả thi.
Đúng — Nathan nói 'the team succeeds or fails together' nên điểm chung là công bằng nhất.
Sai — 'Teachers should not give any marks for projects.': Nathan không phản đối việc chấm điểm dự án.
Sai — 'Students prefer working alone to working in a team.': Không ai nói học sinh thích làm một mình hơn.

questions.prompt: What does the speaker C mean by 'offers moral support'?
choices: The student helps the others write the slides.
The student is the most honest member of the team.
The student in question contributes almost nothing practical.
The student leads the group very well.
questions.explanation: 'Offers moral support' là cách nói mỉa mai về người không làm việc.
choiceExplanations: Sai — 'The student helps the others write the slides.': C nói người làm slide là người thức đến hai giờ sáng, không phải người này.
Sai — 'The student is the most honest member of the team.': Không có chi tiết nào về sự trung thực của người này.
Đúng — C mỉa mai người ngồi cuối lớp 'who does nothing' nhưng chỉ cổ vũ tinh thần.
Sai — 'The student leads the group very well.': C ngụ ý anh ta không đóng góp thực sự.

questions.prompt: True, False, or Not given? Speaker C stayed up past two in the morning to finish her slides.
choices: True
False
Not given
questions.explanation: C nói mình hoàn thành lúc 'ten past two, not two', tức là sau hai giờ sáng.
choiceExplanations: Đúng — C tự sửa thành 'ten past two', tức là sau hai giờ sáng.
Sai — 'False': C nói rõ là hai giờ mười phút, muộn hơn hai giờ.
Sai — 'Not given': Bài nêu rõ giờ C hoàn thành.

questions.prompt: How does Nathan's position change by the end?
choices: He shifts from equal grades toward trusting teachers' overall judgment.
He abandons his views and agrees with the hybrid form.
He insists that nothing about his view has changed.
He says the audience should decide the grading system.
questions.explanation: Từ bảo vệ điểm chung, Nathan chuyển sang bảo vệ đánh giá tổng thể của giáo viên.
choiceExplanations: Đúng — C nhận xét 'you're defending the teacher's judgment' và Nathan đáp 'Perhaps I am'.
Sai — 'He abandons his views and agrees with the hybrid form.': Nathan vẫn chê hình thức bản tự đánh giá là khó tin cậy.
Sai — 'He insists that nothing about his view has changed.': Anh thừa nhận 'Perhaps I am', tức là đã đổi trọng tâm.
Sai — 'He says the audience should decide the grading system.': Chỉ người điều phối mời khán giả phát biểu; Nathan không nói vậy.

title: Podcast về ứng dụng học từ do học sinh làm
transcript:
A: Today's guests are Jonas and Priya, the two students behind a vocabulary app that, I'm told, half of ninth grade now uses. Jonas, you're the one who had the idea?
B: Technically, yes. Although it came from an argument. Priya said memorizing lists was a waste of time, and I said it wasn't, so we decided to settle it by building something.
C: And we both lost, as it turned out, because the first version was dreadful. It showed one word at a time and then asked you to type it from memory. People complained it felt like being interrogated by a toaster.
A: A toaster. That's a first for this show.
B: We took it as constructive feedback. So in the second version we added short example sentences, and a little game where the words fall from the top of the screen.
C: Which is fun for about five minutes. Then you notice that some of the sentences we wrote are, shall we say, mysterious. One of them says, and I quote, "The elephant was extremely persuasive."
A: Is that wrong?
B: Not wrong. Just surprisingly specific. We left it in. It's the most popular sentence in the app.
A: Are you making money from it?
C: Not a cent, and I want to be clear that this is by choice. We did get an offer from a company, and they wanted to add advertisements, but we said no.
B: Mostly because we couldn't agree on where the advertisements would go. Which, if I'm honest, is a pretty good reason to stay independent.
A: What are your plans?
B: Next term we want teachers to be able to add their own word lists. After that, who knows? Possibly a version for younger kids.
C: Possibly. But I'd like to get through exams first. I told Jonas that the app has already taken more of my evenings than the whole of last year's science course.
B: And yet she's the one who keeps finding new bugs at midnight.
C: Somebody has to.

questions.prompt: What does 'interrogated by a toaster' tell us about the first version?
choices: Users found it cold and unfriendly to use.
It was difficult to repair when it broke.
It was too fast for people to follow.
It was designed for kitchen use.
questions.explanation: Hình ảnh hài hước ngụ ý ứng dụng đầu tiên rất gượng ép, khó chịu.
choiceExplanations: Đúng — Người dùng chê nó như bị thẩm vấn bởi cái máy nướng bánh: cứng nhắc, khô khan.
Sai — 'It was difficult to repair when it broke.': Câu so sánh nói về cảm giác khi dùng, không phải việc sửa chữa.
Sai — 'It was too fast for people to follow.': Phản hồi nói về cách hỏi bài, không phải tốc độ.
Sai — 'It was designed for kitchen use.': Đây là cách nói hài hước, không nói về nhà bếp.

questions.prompt: Why is the sentence about the persuasive elephant special?
choices: It is grammatically wrong and will be removed.
It was written by a teacher who joined later.
It is strange, yet it has become the most popular one.
It teaches a very difficult word for exams.
questions.explanation: Câu lạ nhưng được yêu thích nhất.
choiceExplanations: Sai — 'It is grammatically wrong and will be removed.': Jonas nói 'Not wrong' và họ đã giữ lại.

title: Bản tin radio của trường: đổi lịch và vài lời trêu
transcript:
A: Good morning, and welcome to Lunchtime Live, the only radio show in school that is broadcast to a canteen where nobody can hear it.
B: Which is a shame, because today we have actual news. First, the sports day, previously scheduled for Friday the ninth, has been moved to the sixteenth, because of the forecast.
A: Which, I'd like to point out, says sunshine. But apparently the principal doesn't trust the weather forecast any more than I trust the soup.
B: Careful. The soup has feelings. Anyway, the change means that Friday the ninth is now an ordinary school day. Yes, I know. Take a moment.
A: Moving on to the library. Mrs. Okafor asks me to remind you that the books due last month are still due. They did not forget; they were merely waiting.
B: That's a very polite way of saying they know where you live.
A: Next, the drama club. Their autumn play is called The Last Train, and tickets are four dollars for students, or five for everyone else. Correction, I'm told it's six for everyone else, which, frankly, is a bargain for anyone who has paid to see a school play before.
B: Do not say that near the drama club.
A: I would never. And now a notice that I was handed on a very crumpled piece of paper. Someone has found a pair of glasses with a blue case near the science wing. If they're yours, go to the front office. If they're not yours, please stop trying them on.
B: And finally, an announcement from the student council. This term's suggestion box will be emptied every Monday, and, I quote, "all reasonable suggestions will be read aloud at the next meeting."
A: Note the word reasonable. I submitted a suggestion for a swimming pool on the roof, and I haven't heard anything.
B: I wonder why.
A: Well, that's all for today. Join us next week, when we will be discussing the most important question facing our school: whether the cafeteria's pizza is, in fact, a pizza.
B: This is Lunchtime Live. Eat well, if you can.

title: Dặn dò trong phòng thí nghiệm và một học sinh hay cãi
transcript:
A: Before anybody touches anything, I'd like everyone to hear the instructions once, from start to finish. Yes, even you, Kai.
B: I was only going to look at the microscope.
A: Looking is how it begins. Right. Today's practical is about onion cells. First, you take one thin piece of onion skin, and by thin I mean almost invisible, and place it flat on the glass slide. If it folds over, start again. Second, add a single drop of the blue liquid with the dropper. One. Not three.
B: Why only one drop? Wouldn't more make it clearer?
A: Good question, and the answer is the opposite. Too much liquid and the skin floats around, and you'll spend half an hour chasing it. Third, lower a cover glass at an angle, slowly, so you don't trap air bubbles. Bubbles look like cells to the untrained eye, and they have ruined more reports than carelessness.
B: But they said carelessness was the main cause last year.
A: Did they? I'm not sure who "they" is, but I'm confident the bubbles are at least a close second. Now, the part I'm going to repeat: wipe up every spill immediately, and wash your hands before leaving. The blue liquid is harmless, but it stains clothes for good.
B: Is it dangerous to eat?
A: Kai, why would you ask that?
B: Curiosity.
A: Then keep it as curiosity, please. Finally, when you look through the microscope, start with the smallest lens, the one with the short barrel, and only move to the bigger one when you have the cells in focus. Turning the big lens in too soon is the quickest way to crack a slide, and the school has exactly six spare ones.
B: Six? Last term you said ten.
A: I did say ten. Then somebody dropped four. I will not name names, but I will say that the person I'm thinking of is not standing at this table.
B: That's reassuring. Can we start?
A: You may begin. And Kai, one drop.

title: Phỏng vấn tác giả truyện thiếu niên về việc sửa bản thảo
transcript:
A: My guest today is Leo Marsh, whose novel for teenagers, The Salt Road, has just been published. Leo, people always imagine authors writing in bursts of inspiration. Is that how it worked?
B: I wish. The honest answer is that the first draft was terrible. It was nearly nine hundred pages, and about two hundred of them were a character describing the weather.
A: Nine hundred? The finished book is, what, three hundred and twenty?
B: Three hundred and ten, actually. My editor trimmed ten pages at the very end because of a printing issue, and I'm still not sure I forgive her.
A: So what did the revising look like?
B: Mostly cutting. I used to believe every sentence was precious, and I'd spend a week saving a paragraph that nobody needed. Then I read the draft aloud to my younger brother, and by page twelve he was asleep. That was a more useful review than anything a critic has written.
A: Did you ever consider giving up?
B: Constantly. Not because the writing was hard, but because it was boring. Fixing a book is a lot less glamorous than inventing one. You sit there with a pencil asking, does this scene earn its place? And it usually doesn't.
A: Is there a scene you miss?
B: One. There was a chapter in which the two main characters get lost in a market, and it was the funniest thing I'd ever written. It had nothing to do with the plot, so it had to go. I keep it in a drawer and read it when I'm sad.
A: That sounds painful.
B: It was, for about a week, and then I realized the book was better without it. Painful and correct are often the same thing in revision.
A: Any advice for young writers?
B: Finish something. Anything. Most people think the hard part is having ideas, but ideas are cheap. The hard part is staying with one long enough to make it good, and being willing to throw away what you love.
A: Leo Marsh, thank you.

title: Thảo luận về các ngôn ngữ đang biến mất
transcript:
A: Our topic today is the idea that languages are disappearing, and whether we should try to stop it. Ivan, you wanted to start.
B: Yes. I'll admit I used to think this was sad but inevitable, like losing a dialect of a village you've never visited. Then I read about a language that is spoken by a few elderly people in a single valley, and has words for kinds of snow that no other language has bothered to name.
C: But isn't that precisely the argument that makes me uneasy? Words for snow. It sounds charming, but if the children of that valley would rather speak a bigger language, to find work, to use the internet, who are we to complain?
B: Nobody is complaining about their choice. The question is whether it's really a free choice. If a school only teaches in the larger language, the children aren't choosing, they're being steered.
C: Fair. Though steering happens everywhere. I learned English at school and I don't feel robbed.
B: You learned English in addition to your own language. That's the point. Nobody is asking anyone to give up the useful language; the issue is the loss of the other one.
A: Let me bring in a practical question. Who would pay for keeping a language alive?
C: Exactly my worry. Recording dictionaries and making teaching materials costs a lot, and the money usually has to come from somewhere with other priorities.
B: Though a recording costs relatively little compared with what's lost if it's never made. Once the last speaker is gone, no amount of money brings it back.
C: I accept that. But my doubt remains about whether a recorded language is a living one. A language in a museum is not really the same as a language in a kitchen.
B: I couldn't agree more, which is why I think the best projects are the ones that put the language back in the kitchen, where grandparents teach grandchildren.
A: So you both want the language to continue, but you disagree about how much effort the rest of us should give it.
C: That's a perfectly fair summary, and slightly annoying.
B: I'd say it's accurate.

title: Buổi ngắm sao bị hủy vì mây
transcript:
A: Good evening, everyone, and thank you for coming. I'm afraid I have some news, and I'd like to deliver it with maximum honesty and minimum drama. The stargazing night is canceled.
B: Canceled? We've been planning it since September.
A: I know, Amir. The cloud cover is, let's say, complete. I've been looking out of the window for forty minutes, and I can report that the sky is a large gray ceiling. Even the moon, which is normally reliable, has decided not to attend.
C: Maybe it will clear later. My uncle says clouds go away after midnight.
A: Your uncle may be right, and I admire his optimism. But I'm not going to keep twenty students outside in the cold at one in the morning on the basis of a family rumor.
B: So what do we do with the telescope?
A: Good question. The school has only one, and it's been very carefully borrowed, so I'm going to lock it away until Thursday, when the forecast looks better. Not Wednesday, as I told some of you earlier, because Wednesday, I'm told, has rain.
C: We could still use the time for something. Maybe an indoor lesson?
A: Now that's an idea I can support. I've brought a set of star maps, and since we're here, we could learn to find the constellations the old-fashioned way, by looking at a piece of paper and pretending.
B: Pretending to look at stars is not exactly the same thing.
A: No. It is, however, what astronomers did for a very long time before telescopes, and a few of them even seemed to enjoy it.
C: Fine. But if Thursday is also cloudy, I want it noted that I predicted a disaster.
A: Noted, Dana. And if Thursday is also cloudy, I will personally take the blame, and bring biscuits.
B: Now you're talking.
A: Right. Maps are on the table by the door. Take one each, and please, no folding them into airplanes. They belong to the physics department, and the physics department is not known for its sense of humor.

title: Ba người bàn về nuôi ong trên mái trường
transcript:
A: The proposal is simple. We put two beehives on the roof of the science block, and the biology club looks after them. Honey, pollination, a learning opportunity. What could possibly go wrong?
B: I'll tell you what could go wrong. Somebody is allergic. We have nine hundred students, and I'd be astonished if none of them reacts badly to a sting.
C: That's a legitimate concern, Mr. Dunn, but the hives would be on the roof, with a locked door, and bees don't usually go looking for people. They go looking for flowers.
B: Usually. Which is a word I find very uncomfortable when it comes to something with a sting.
A: Let me offer a different angle. The school has a garden that struggles every summer. Fewer insects visit it than they should. If we had bees, the vegetable beds would do better, and the students would see directly why bees matter.
B: I can see the argument for the garden. I just don't think it needs hives on our own roof. We could ask a local beekeeper to place hives on a farm nearby, and bring the students there for a visit.
C: With respect, that's rather different. Watching a hive from behind a fence isn't the same as learning to look after one. Half the value is in the responsibility.
B: Responsibility. From students who forget their lunches?
C: From students who've asked to do it, in writing, at their own expense. The club has raised enough for the equipment already.
B: Has it? That I did not know. Nobody mentioned money before.
A: It's in the second page of the proposal, just after the section on safety. I'm sure you read it carefully.
B: Of course I read it. I may have read it quickly.
A: Then here's what I suggest. We invite an expert to talk to the staff and to the parents, and we ask any family with a serious allergy to tell us, confidentially. If the risk looks real, we drop the idea. If not, we start with one hive.
B: One hive, not two.
A: One hive. And if all goes well, a second next year.
B: I'll agree to a meeting. I haven't agreed to the bees.

title: Phỏng vấn nhạc công về chuyện thiên bẩm
transcript:
A: Today I'm talking with Marcus Bell, a cellist who started playing at the age of seven and now, at fifteen, plays in the youth orchestra. Marcus, everybody says you're a natural. Does that annoy you?
B: A little, yes. Because natural makes it sound as if I woke up one morning and the cello was just there. The truth is I practiced for forty minutes a day for the first two years, and those forty minutes were often terrible. My mother says the cat left the house.
A: But some people do seem to learn faster than others.
B: Of course. I'm not going to pretend that everyone starts from the same place. But I've noticed that the people who are called talented are usually people who've found something they're willing to be bad at for a long time. That's the difference, not the gift.
A: That's a generous way to put it.
B: It's also convenient, because it means the rest of us can't blame ourselves for lacking a gift. We can only blame ourselves for lacking patience, which is much easier to fix.
A: How do you actually practice?
B: Slowly. Embarrassingly slowly. My teacher says that if I can play a passage at full speed the first time, it was probably too easy. She makes me play the hardest four bars ten times at half the speed, and then she asks me to explain what my fingers were doing.
A: Explain what your fingers were doing?
B: I know. It sounds ridiculous. But if I can describe it, I understand it, and if I understand it, I stop making the same mistake.
A: Do you ever feel like quitting?
B: Last winter, honestly. There was a concert I was dreading, and I wanted to drop out of the orchestra altogether. I didn't, because my friend, who plays the flute, told me she was frightened too. That helped more than any advice.
A: What do you want to do after school?
B: I'd like to say I'm going to be a professional musician, but I'm only fifteen. For now I'd like to keep playing, and maybe study science as well. The cello isn't going anywhere, and it doesn't mind waiting.
A: Marcus, thank you.

title: Phỏng vấn cựu kỳ thủ cờ vua về trực giác
transcript:
A: Joining me in the studio is Mr. Halloran, who taught chess at the community center for many years. Mr. Halloran, a lot of beginners ask whether chess is about calculation or instinct. What do you say?
B: I say the question is slightly unfair, because it presumes the two are enemies. They're more like two people carrying a heavy table. Nobody gets far if one of them walks off.
A: Can you give an example?
B: Imagine you're looking at a position, and you feel that one of the pieces is in the wrong place. You can't say why, but the feeling is strong. That's instinct. Then you test it, move by move, in your head, and sometimes the feeling collapses, and sometimes it holds. That's calculation. Beginners often trust the first completely, or the second completely, and both are mistakes.
A: Which mistake is more common?
B: In children, the first. They play a quick move, announce that it's brilliant, and lose a piece. In adults, the second. They calculate for twenty minutes, find a long line that wins, and miss that the opponent had a simple reply on the first move.
A: Do you have a memory of a game you lost badly?
B: Oh, yes. I played a young girl, perhaps eleven, in a tournament in the nineties. I had been playing for thirty years, or twenty-eight, depending on who counts the years I took off. I was certain I was winning, and she calmly took my queen with a pawn. I stared at the board for a full minute. Then I shook her hand and told her it was a lovely game.
A: Was it?
B: It was a lovely game for her. For me, it was educational. I still tell the story to my students. They enjoy it more than I do.
A: What do you tell a child who is frustrated after losing?
B: That every strong player has lost thousands of games. The losses aren't a sign of failure; they are the training. The ones who improve are the ones who ask, what did I miss? And the ones who don't improve are the ones who say, I was unlucky.
A: Mr. Halloran, thank you very much.
B: Thank you. And if anyone wants to challenge me, I should warn you that I've been practicing.

title: Thông báo của ban tổ chức triển lãm khoa học
transcript:
A: Good afternoon, everybody. This is a short announcement about next week's science exhibition, and I'd like to apologize in advance for any confusion, because I believe I created most of it.
B: Which part, exactly?
A: The part where I told you the exhibition opens at nine. It opens at nine thirty. The doors will be unlocked at nine, for teams to set up, but visitors don't come in until half past.
B: And closing time?
A: Four o'clock. Not five. I mention it because several of you have already booked a bus for five, and I'd hate for the driver to be the only person waiting.
B: What about the judging?
A: Ah, good. The judges will visit each stand between ten and twelve. That is not the same as being at each stand at ten. If you leave your table to find a snack at ten fifteen, you may meet the judges' backs. I strongly recommend that someone from every team stays.
B: Should we bring our own equipment?
A: Yes, for anything electrical. The school will provide tables and one extension cord per team, which sounds generous until you realize there are forty teams.
B: So, essentially, bring your own cord.
A: I've not said that, but I haven't disagreed either. Also, please, no open flames, no liquids that can stain, and no live animals. We discussed this at length at the last meeting, after a certain incident with a hamster.
B: I wasn't aware there was a hamster.
A: Most people weren't, until it left the building. Lastly, prizes. There'll be three, for the best project, the most original idea, and the best explanation. That last one is, in my experience, the hardest. A good presentation isn't about speaking loudly; it's about knowing what a stranger doesn't know.
B: That's quite a thoughtful way to put it.
A: Thank you. I've been waiting all day to say it. Right, I'll see you all on Thursday, at nine, no, at nine thirty. Actually, at nine, if you're setting up.
